newsitem.title: USA: Grains, gold lead commodity index lower.
newsitem.headline: Grains, gold lead commodity index lower.

text.p: Grains and gold led commodity prices lower on Monday, pushing one widely watched price index to a new low for the year.
Gold prices hit 12-year lows for a second straight trading session as weak inflation and this year's sales of gold reserves by central banks fed a bearish mood among speculators.
Wheat prices fell to three-year lows and corn prices sank to their lowest in 2-1/2 years as ideal growing weather in the United States pointed to bumper, and possibly record, crops.
The Commodity Research Bureau's index of 17 futures contracts ended down 3.35 points at 232.22, a new 1997 low.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat for July delivery closed down 6-3/4 cents a bushel at $3.13-1/2.
"Yields have been very good in the winter areas and the showers will help the spring wheat," said Tom Levis, analyst for Prudential Securities.
In corn, the largest grain crop, the futures contract for post-harvest delivery in December closed 4 cents lower at $2.29-1/2, after setting a new life-of-contract low.
The market remained overwhelmed with mild temperatures and occasional rainfall in the key U.S. corn growing states.
"It's getting to be old hat, contract lows again," Levis said. "It's mostly weather, and in fact everything looks fantastic. It's getting close to pollination and no problems yet."

Some Chicago grain analysts were beginning to talk about a potential 10 billion bushel corn crop this year, assuming the weather remains conducive for pollination and ear-filling in August. A record 10.1 billion bushels were produced in 1994.

Soybeans for harvest delivery also fell, with November futures ending down 7-3/4 cents a bushel at $5.84-1/4. But soybeans for delivery this month bucked the lower trend on concerns that existing supplies may be squeezed.
July soybeans ended at $7.32-3/4, up 10-3/4 cents.

"We've got 40 million bushels of open interest (outstanding contracts) in the July. We've got 2.6 million available for delivery," said Bill Biedermann, director of agricultural research at Allendale Inc. in McHenry, Illinois.
Ideal growing weather also fed selling in cotton futures, with December cotton at the New York Cotton Exchange closing down 2.05 cents a pound at 73.75 cents after hitting a new life-of-contract low.
Beneficial rains for cotton fell over the weekend in west Texas, Georgia and Alabama, key producing areas.
In New York, gold prices dropped to fresh 12-year lows, with August gold at the COMEX closing at $319.00, down $6.20 an ounce.

The losses came on the heels of a $7 drop last Thursday after Australia's central bank said it had sold most of its gold reserves. U.S. markets were closed to trading on Friday in observance of the Independence Day holiday.
The selloff was a continuation of a well-established downward trend in gold prices as a growing number of central banks confirmed having sold the metal, dealers said.
"Underneath $300 is entirely possible," said Scott Mehlman, chief dealer at Credit Lyonnais Rouse. "There may be some short-covering rallies, but they will be worth selling."
COMEX September silver tumbled more than 30 cents to $4.25 an ounce, the lowest in just over four years, before recovering to end at $4.285 an ounce, down 28.5 cents.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil prices ended lower on concerns that Iraq will soon submit its aid distribution plan to the United Nations and resume exporting oil under its accord with the U.N..

"The topic of conversation seems to be when Iraq will submit its aid distribution plan. We are going to be consolidating within a range until it finally happens," said Tim Evans, an analyst with Pegasus Econometric Group in New York.
Crude oil for August delivery closed 4 cents lower at $19.52 a barrel. Monday's decline followed a 78-cent decline in crude last Thursday on the same concerns.
In May, the U.N. renewed a plan whereby Iraq can sell $2 billion of oil every six months on a renewable basis to buy food, medicine and other humanitarian supplies.
The second six-month phase of oil sales would have started June 8 but has been held up pending completion by Iraq's government of new distribution plan for the food and other goods.
August heating oil closed 0.02 cent a gallon higher at 52.78 cents and August unleaded gasoline ended 0.02 higher at 57.94 cents.
